cultural.vision_reason: An ancient Egyptian ivory/stone cosmetic comb carved with a recumbent gazelle atop the comb teeth, a New Kingdom toiletry object consistent with Egyptian material culture.

physical.title: Comb with Gazelle
physical.summary: Both ancient Egyptian men and women loved cosmetics. Unguents, oils, and perfumes made from aromatic plant resins and gums were obtained at great cost from distant lands. The objects identified with cosmetics were given lavish treatment. The luxurious obsidian and gold beaker hints at the precious contents it once held. Others are fanciful in form, such as an ostrich egg. The god Bes, patron god of cosmetics, himself is the subject of a colorful jar. The delicately carved human face and the head of a giraffe decorated elaborate ivory cosmetic spoons.

location.made_in_place: Egypt, New Kingdom (1540–1069 BCE), Dynasty 18, reign of Amenhotep III (1390–1352 BCE)
